name: Aaron Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at a firm of about forty people in the city, on the second floor above a bank, and I do year-end accounts and tax returns for small charities, a few cafés and a lot of tradespeople. Most mornings I'm matching bank statements to receipts that come in as a carrier bag of paper, honestly. I like the charities best, because the treasurers are retired teachers who bring biscuits and actually care where every pound goes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: January wears me out, when every plumber in the city remembers his tax return at once. What I like is getting a set of accounts to balance by hand, in my own spreadsheet, and knowing every number in it. The firm brought in an AI assistant last spring and I've never opened it, which my manager Carol jokes about at every team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest, mostly to Dev, who I eat lunch with and who keeps sending me articles about robots replacing us. Online I wouldn't say much, I'm not on there a lot. At work I'd just say good, now can we stop having training sessions about a tool nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing really changes, and I'm fine with that. I earn well for my level, I've got about ten months of savings, and there are firms hiring on every street near the office. If the bank feeds get a bit smarter at sorting receipts, that's a small bit of my day, not my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and sit my tax specialist exam next autumn like I planned. I'd keep putting a fifth of my pay into savings each month. Leah and I would probably start looking at buying a flat together in the next year or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mainly. I'd feel like the people who stuck to doing the work properly were right. A bit smug too, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the routine bits might change a little. Which part of your day would that touch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank matching, probably, the carrier bag of receipts part. I've seen the software file a vet's bill as a restaurant meal. I'd still check whatever it sorted. So maybe an hour a week saved, and I'd spend it on the charity accounts I actually enjoy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work or money that worries you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, if I'm fair. The firm's busy, my pay went up in April, and Leah's job on the children's ward isn't going anywhere. The only thing is the hours in January, which nobody's software ever fixed.

say: I'd say the **AI hype** was overblown and we can stop the training sessions.
I'd tell Dev at lunch that doing the work **properly** was the right call.
think: Privately I think **nothing much** changes for me, and I'm glad.
My **ten months** of savings and plenty of local jobs mean I'm secure.
do: Sit the **tax specialist exam** next autumn as already planned.
Keep saving a **fifth of pay** each month into the savings account.
Start looking at **buying a flat** with Leah within a year or so.
feel: **Relieved** that the careful way of working still counts.
A little **smug** towards the colleagues who rushed to new tools.
S0.quote: I've seen the software file a vet's bill as a restaurant meal. I'd still check whatever it sorted.
fieldNote: Aaron's calm rests on **real security**: strong savings, a recent pay rise and many firms nearby.
He frames the plateau as a **vindication** of careful, hand-built work.
The January workload is his only standing **pressure**, and it has nothing to do with AI.

steps.text: Sit the tax specialist exam next autumn
Put a fifth of each month's pay into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need to slow down and talk about who this is for, because it won't be for us. I'd probably bring it up at the union branch, the staff union a few of us joined last year. Online I might share a post about the big firms cutting graduate intakes, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a person who refuses to touch the software is the obvious one to let go, and on my floor that person is me. If the software does the bank matching, the drafting and the checking, there's not much left that needs me. Carol has already said the new hires will be half what they were, and I'm average at this job, not a star.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself sit the AI course the firm keeps offering, even if I hate it, in the first month. I'd ask to move fully onto the charity clients, because the treasurers want a person at the table. And I'd push the union branch to get a written promise that nobody is let go without retraining first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first and then properly worried, like when you notice your name isn't on the rota. I feel a bit stupid for being so stubborn. And angry that the partners will keep the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sit the course even though you hate it. Would you actually use the tool afterwards?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably only the bits I can check line by line. I'd let it draft the covering letters and I'd still tick every figure myself. Carol would say that's half using it, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, oddly, because he's keen on all this but he's the newest on our team. And the two bookkeepers on the ground floor, who do exactly the matching the software is built for. They've got kids and a lot less saved than me.

say: I'd say the gains should go to **staff**, not only to the partners.
I'd raise the firm's **hiring cuts** at our staff union branch.
think: As the one who **refuses AI**, I'd be the obvious person to cut.
Being **average** at the job leaves me little shelter if teams shrink.
do: Take the firm's **AI course** in the first month, despite hating it.
Ask to move fully onto **charity clients**, where people want a person.
Push the union for a **written promise** of retraining before any cuts.
feel: **Worried**, like noticing my name is missing from the rota.
**Angry** that the partners will keep the savings from the software.
S1.quote: A person who refuses to touch the software is the obvious one to let go, and on my floor that person is me.
fieldNote: He sees his own **resistance** to AI as his main weak spot here.
His progressive views show in turning first to the **union branch**.
Concern shifts quickly to **lower-paid** bookkeepers with thinner savings than his.

steps.text: Take the firm's AI course in the first month
Ask Carol to move him fully onto charity clients
Push the union branch for a no-cuts-without-retraining promise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal that it was let loose with no plan, and I'd say it loudly. I'd go to whatever march there is about it, I think. At work there wouldn't be much to say, because there'd barely be work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm out of a job within the year it arrives. Everything I do is at a desk: tax returns, accounts, letters. The only bit of hands-on in my week is carrying the carrier bags of receipts upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before it lands, I'd stop saving for a flat and keep the money as cash, all of it. I'd look hard at the hands-on jobs that buy me those three years before the robots, maybe training as a maths teaching assistant or something in a school. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income, because I don't see another answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the floor's tilted. I keep thinking about all those exam nights for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Leah that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend that her nursing job just became the one paying the rent. Then I'd probably apologise, which is daft. She'd tell me to stop it and make tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned school work. Why that, rather than staying in finance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a classroom full of eleven-year-olds still needs a grown-up in it, whatever the software can do. I did maths tutoring at university and I liked it. It's not a plan so much as the only door I can see from here.

say: I'd call it a **scandal** that it arrived with no plan at all.
I'd go to a **march** and back a basic income in public.
think: I expect to **lose my job** within a year of it arriving.
My work is all **desk work**, so the robot delay doesn't help me.
do: Pause the **flat purchase** and keep all savings as cash.
Look into **school work**, like a maths teaching assistant role.
Join campaigns for a **basic income** in the first year.
feel: **Sick**, as if the floor had tilted under me.
**Bitter** about the years of exam nights.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend that her nursing job just became the one paying the rent.
fieldNote: He sees **no buffer** from the robot delay, since his work is all screens.
His strong savings turn from a house deposit into a **lifeboat**.
Teaching appeals because a classroom still needs a **human adult**, and he has tutoring experience.

steps.text: Put the flat deposit on hold and keep it as cash
Apply for maths teaching assistant jobs at local schools
Join a basic income campaign and go to its marches

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd say it while we still have time to do something. I'd tell the union branch that five years is enough to fight for a proper deal. Online I'd post that this is a choice about who gets the money, not the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years buys me something, but not much, because I'm still all desk work. I'd be thirty-two when it lands, and every firm would stop training juniors well before that. I think the job is gone for me either way; the only question is whether I've got something else ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time teaching qualification next September and keep working at the firm while I do it. I'd still buy the flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage is something Leah could cover on her own. And I'd push hard at the union for a redundancy deal that pays for retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Five years is like being told about a flood five years out. You sandbag, but you know the water's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a flat. Isn't that a risk if you think the job goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but renting's a risk too, and Leah's job is hands-on. We'd buy something with one bedroom near her hospital rather than the two-bed we wanted. If the mortgage fits her pay alone, I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to actually use the AI tools in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably seeing Dev get promoted for it, which would annoy me into it. I'd learn just enough to train other people on it, because that might be a job for a couple of years. After that I don't know.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** to win a fair deal.
I'd post that this is a choice about **who gets** the money.
think: My job still **goes**, since all of my work is at a desk.
Firms will stop **training juniors** well before the five years are up.
do: Start a **part-time teaching qualification** next September.
Buy a **smaller flat** that Leah's pay alone could cover.
Push the union for **redundancy pay** that funds retraining.
feel: **Heavy**, like being warned about a flood years ahead.
A little **steadier** than with two years, because there's time to sandbag.
S3.quote: Five years is like being told about a flood five years out. You sandbag, but you know the water's coming.
fieldNote: The extra years change his **plans** but not his **outlook** on the job.
He sizes the mortgage so his partner's **hands-on** pay can carry it alone.
Peer rivalry, not conviction, is what might push him to **learn the tools**.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time teaching qualification next September
Buy a one-bed flat near Leah's hospital, not a two-bed
Push the union for redundancy pay that funds retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for a government that doesn't plan. I'd write to my local representative, which I've never done in my life. At work I'd tell the younger ones not to sit the exams I sat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to have a whole second career, which is strange to say out loud. I think I'd keep my job for maybe six or seven of those years, and then it shrinks to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for now and keep saving hard. Somewhere in the next two years I'd start the teaching qualification properly, full-time, and live off savings and Leah while I train. I'd also want us to have our first kid before the change, not after, which we'd never really talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, still, but there's room to breathe. It feels like I'd be choosing, not being pushed. That matters to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you tell the younger ones not to sit the exams?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the accountancy exams are three years of evenings, and they teach you exactly what the software will do. I'd tell them to go into something with people in the room. Dev would argue, he always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the job six or seven years. What makes you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Clients like my charity treasurers trust slowly. They'll want a person signing things off long after the software could. But I know that's a guess, and it's a hopeful one.

say: I'd say a decade leaves **no excuse** for poor government planning.
I'd tell younger colleagues to skip the **accountancy exams** I sat.
think: At **thirty-seven** I'd still have time for a full second career.
I'd guess the job lasts **six or seven** years before shrinking away.
do: Keep **saving hard** while staying at the firm for now.
Train full-time as a **teacher** within two years, living off savings.
Bring forward plans for a **first child** before the change lands.
feel: **Worried**, but with room to breathe and choose.
Some **pride** at deciding my own path instead of being pushed.
S4.quote: The accountancy exams are three years of evenings, and they teach you exactly what the software will do.
fieldNote: Ten years turns his fear into a **chosen** career change.
Writing to his **representative** would be a first for him.
He admits his six-to-seven-year job estimate is a **hopeful** guess based on trusting clients.

steps.text: Keep saving a fifth of pay while still at the firm
Train full-time as a maths teacher within two years
Write to his local representative about a retraining plan
Plan a first child with Leah before the change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd have no second skill ready and nothing in my hands. What would help is paid retraining, real money while you train, like an apprenticeship wage for grown-ups. And a basic income so people like the bookkeepers downstairs aren't left with nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd still choose accounting, knowing all this. I wouldn't. I'd have gone into teaching at twenty-two, and I'd have been happier on less money.

headlineQuote: I'd have gone into teaching at twenty-two, and I'd have been happier on less money.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** accountant doing tax and accounts for charities, cafés and tradespeople at a forty-person firm.
He has never opened the firm's **AI assistant** and prefers ticking every figure himself.
His **strong savings** and his girlfriend's nursing job make him secure in the plateau and calmer than most.
From Steady Disruption on, he sees his **resistance** as his weak spot and turns to the union.
In the AGI pictures he plans to **retrain as a teacher**, sooner the faster it comes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no second skill and only desk work to offer.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** with a living wage while people train.
A **basic income** for lower-paid staff with less saved than him.
